questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The two most important aspects to me were the that the study destination should have relevant courses to my study programme such that I could further my skills, and.. nature and mountains! The University of British Columbia fulfilled both those criteria as they offer a good selection of environmental / climate related courses taught at an equivalent level to that of KU, and the nature that surrounds Vancouver is astonishing.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Practically all the required information was e-mailed prior to arrival or during the introduction week. I did not find that I was missing information regarding my studies or living conditions, etc.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
There was no particular assistance provided upon arrival. From the airport you can make your own way to the university / accommodation, where check-in occurs by going to the common block / reception of your assigned residence. There you would get a folder with informative papers and your key.

That aside, the introduction week contained a lot of informative and social events to kick things off, while most of the important/mandatory information regarding classes was delivered by e-mail and through Canvas (Absalon).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: UBC has an assortment of on-campus residencies. As part of the application process students can choose to apply for residence at UBC. In that application you rank the dorms (1 to 10) according to where you would prefer to stay, but in reality the vast majority of exchange students that are assigned a residence will end up at Walter Gage or Fairview Crescent. Important to note that far from everyone who applies will receive a spot in a residence. There were many exchange students that had to find their own accommodation in Vancouver.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: No meal plans were offered, but apartments both in Walter Gage and Fairview Crescent had kitchens equipped with an oven/stove and fridge/freezer, but without utensils and equipment of any sort.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Most importantly, on-campus housing is not a certainty, and finding short-term accommodation in Vancouver can be difficult and expensive. I'd highly recommend applying for on-campus living whilst also weighing up other options / getting in contact with other exchange students about potentially renting a place together.

On-campus housing provides a good opportunity to meet a lot of exchange students and at Fairview Crescent we often had social activities planned by the Resident Advisors which gave good community vibes.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The registration process is rather lengthy and begins with your application. For pre-approval you may only need 30 ECTS, but for the UBC application you are required to list at least 10 courses you could potentially register for. The actual registration for courses happens over summer and is done by filling out an online form sent by UBC. In the form you fill out information about the courses you want, and rank them by most to least wanted courses. It is not certain that you get all your most wanted courses.

For Masters students the process is a bit more complicated as it involves contacting the course instructors to receive permission to join their courses.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Information about course registration was both e-mailed and we also had a zoom presentation / meeting in which UBC went over the process and the important deadlines. That aside one is free to contact UBC for more help during the process if needed.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: All the courses I ended up taking were ones I wanted, but not all my top-ranked ones. One of my courses were also cancelled upon arrival.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
I think it is important to note that when looking at courses for pre-approval, be aware of what term (1 or 2) the course is offered, what timeslot it is assigned, whether exchange students are eligible for it, and what level (100-500) it is, and of course what campus it is offered at (Okanagan or Vancouver).

Register for more courses than you need ECTS. It is easy to drop out of a course once you arrive (within first two weeks) through an online form, and some courses may be cancelled (especially higher level courses that have fewer students).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The academic level of the courses felt equivalent to that offered at KU.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The style of teaching depends heavily on the lecturer and the course that you are taking. Common for all of the courses, however, is that they require a lot more weekly interaction than those at KU. There will typically be weekly readings, quizzes, case studies/small tasks, etc., that are mandatory and count toward your final grade (roughly 20% of grades are made up of "participation" type activities such as those listed).

If you are used to hanging back and cramming for a final exam that counts 100%, then this will feel quite different and perhaps a bit more "high-school" like. There are also midterms (either one or two) that count for some 20% each. The upside is that the final exam typically only accounts for 30 percent of your grade and therefore feels pretty relaxed.

Style of teaching will also depend on what type of class it is. In the course descriptions it will be denoted whether it is a "lecture", "lab", "hybrid", etc., style class. Some are interactive and require a lot of group work while others are mostly traditional lectures.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Environmental Impact Assessment
Global Climate Change
Environmental Philosophy

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I think that all three courses were interesting in their own way.

Environmental Impact Assessment was a great course with an enthusiastic professor and involved a lot of group work and hands-on assignments with EIA. It is focused on the Canadian law / process, and there are a lot of interesting developments to follow, especially within climate change and indigenous rights. If you want a course that provides tangible (work-related) skills, this is a good one.

Global Climate Change provides a basic overview of the Earth System and deals with a lot of radiation balance calculations. If you've taken Climate Change Mechanisms and Tipping Points I would not necessarily recommend this course, unless you want a more math-heavy approach to understanding the mechanisms.

Environmental Philosophy followed an entire course book on different philosophical approaches / stances on environmental issues. It is a great course for learning how to rationally argue for certain environmental stances, and to ground them in logical reasoning.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did not really encounter any unexpected costs. There are spontaneous trips that you may go on with other exchange students, and those costs can be difficult to plan for precisely.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Overall the price level in Vancouver is very similar to Copenhagen. Groceries are perhaps a bit more expensive in Vancouver, especially if you are vegetarian.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
UBC has a huge selection of clubs to join. During the introduction week there is a club-day where all the clubs set up a booth and you can walk around and hear a little bit about what they have to offer. There are sports clubs (sailing, weightlifting, swimming, dragon-boating, martial arts, running, hiking, climbing, surfing, etc.) and more cultural/social clubs (movies, boardgames, environmental activism, chess, majong, science, etc.). It is highly likely you'll find a fun club to join if you're keen!

I was part of the Varsity Outdoor Club and highly recommend it to anyone who is interested in all outdoors activities (hiking, skiing, biking, climbing). It is student run and volunteer based, so all events are hosted by fellow students. It is a great way to meet locals and other exchange students, and explore the beautiful British Columbia!

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Definitely go out in nature, in whichever way you prefer. British Columbia offers some of the most incredible nature you'll experience, and Vancouver is a hotspot for outdoorsy folks, so there will be no lack of opportunities to come by. There are loads of great hiking trails, some of them very challenging, that offer incredible views. It is also possible to mountain bike, climb, kayak, cave, surf, ski, etc.

Whale watching is also a great experience - you are very likely to spot some humpbacks, and if lucky, some orcas as well!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Visit the Museum of Anthropology on UBC. Go on a micro-brewery bar crawl. Hike up to Garibaldi Lake or Panorama Ridge.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: There is barely any adjustment needed. Given that everyone speaks English, there is no language barrier present, and culturally there are not any significant differences that should make it difficult to adjust to.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Chat with the people you sit next to in class - be open and take initiative to do things post class if you vibe with someone. Joining a club, or several, is probably the easiest way to meet likeminded locals that are likely interested in social activities.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There weren't really any cultural differences that I found challenging. If anything, tipping culture is the thing that stands out the most, but you get used to that pretty quickly.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: For Vancouver particularly I really appreciated the love for the outdoors. It was super easy to meet people that were enthusiastic about outdoor adventuring.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Bring all your outdoor equipment if you are into hiking / camping - you are going to need it, and buying it in Van isn't necessarily cheaper! Go explore all that BC has to offer.

2. If you want the most out of the social life, be a social butterfly! UBC is a massive campus and there are a lot of people. You can easily drown in the masses if you don't take initiative and engage in the clubs / social groups / residence activities. Exchange moves fast, stay on top of your academics so that you can say yes to all the fun activities!

3. Make friends with someone who has a car, haha. You're going to need it. EVO car share is a good alternative to owning a car, but if you want to truly venture out into the wilderness, you'll need a car or know someone with one!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Exploring British Columbia with a bunch of good people. The ease with which one can be out in complete wilderness during the weekend is incredible and makes all the academic work during the week all the more rewarding.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
I think that the academic system is sufficiently different from the Danish one that it can be a challenge to adjust to it. The week-to-week workload will feel more significant because there are a lot of small assignments that are graded. It isn't that the academic content is more difficult, it is just that all these small tasks and deadlines will shape your time more so than at KU.

Stay up to date with the academics and it won't be an issue, but it can feel more difficult to recover from a setback.
